lessons.title: Price vs Intrinsic Value: What a Valuation Is Actually Telling You

children.text: Open Zerodha Kite on any trading day and every stock has a price, updated to the paisa. What no app shows you is what that business is worth. That number, intrinsic value, is what this entire course is about. Before you build a single DCF or compare a single P/E, you need to be precise about the difference between the two, because almost every expensive mistake in equity investing starts with treating them as the same thing.
Price Is a Fact. Value Is an Estimate.
Price
is the last traded price on NSE or BSE. It is set by the most eager buyer and the most eager seller in that moment. It is exact, public and changes every second the market is open.
Intrinsic value

is what the business is worth to an owner, based on the cash it will generate over its remaining life, adjusted for how risky and how distant that cash is. It is not quoted anywhere. You have to estimate it, and two careful analysts will get different answers.

markDefs.definition: The estimated worth of a business or share, based on the cash it is expected to generate for its owners over its remaining life, discounted back to today.

columns.label: Price
points: Set by: buyers and sellers on NSE and BSE
Precision: exact, to the paisa
Changes: every second the market is open
Driven by: news, fund flows, sentiment and liquidity
Where you find it: any broker app or screener.in

columns.label: Intrinsic value
points: Set by: the cash the business generates for its owners
Precision: a range, never a single number
Changes: only when the business outlook changes
Driven by: cash flows, growth and risk
Where you find it: nowhere, you have to estimate it

body.text: The stock price tells you what the market will pay today. A valuation tells you what the business is worth if your assumptions are right. Investing happens in the gap between the two.

children.text: A related trap:
market capitalisation

is not value either. It is simply price multiplied by shares outstanding. When a headline says a company "lost ₹50,000 crore in value" in a day, it lost ₹50,000 crore of market cap. Its plants, customers and cash flows are usually exactly where they were the evening before.

markDefs.definition: Share price multiplied by total shares outstanding. It is the market's current price for the whole of a company's equity, not an estimate of its worth.

children.text: Where Intrinsic Value Comes From

A share is a claim on a business's future cash. Nothing else. Not the logo, not the brand ambassador, not the price chart. As an owner, what you ultimately receive is either cash the company pays out, or the price someone else pays you for the share, and that price should itself depend on the cash still to come.

Cash in the future is worth less than cash today for two reasons: you could have invested it elsewhere in the meantime, and there is a chance it never arrives. So each future amount is shrunk back to today using a
discount rate

markDefs.definition: The annual return you require for waiting and for bearing the risk that the cash may not arrive. A higher discount rate produces a lower present value.

body.caption: Value today = present value of cash received over n years + present value of the expected sale price at year n

children.text: Here V₀ is value today, CFₜ is the cash you receive in year t, r is your required return, and Pₙ is what you expect the share to be worth at the end of year n. Chapters 2 and 3 break down every piece of this formula. For now, watch it work on one share.
Worked Example: One Share of Tarangini Cold Chain

Tarangini Cold Chain Ltd is a fictional NSE-listed company running refrigerated warehouses for seafood and pharma exporters along the western coast. You expect it to generate free cash flow of ₹20 per share next year, rising by ₹2 every year after that, and you believe the share will be worth about ₹400 at the end of year five. Because it is a mid-sized logistics business with some customer concentration, you require a 12% annual return.

body.caption: Tarangini Cold Chain: intrinsic value per share at a 12% required return (illustrative)

stats.label: Value from the year-5 sale price

children.text: Look at the second stat. Nearly three quarters of the value rests on one assumption about year five. That is normal for real businesses, not a quirk of this example, and Chapter 3 shows you how to handle it.
Change one assumption, change the answer
Your 12% required return is a judgement call. An investor who sees Tarangini as safer might use 10%. A more cautious one might use 14%. Same cash flows, same business, three different values.

body.title: Tarangini Cold Chain: intrinsic value per share by required return

body.text: A 2 percentage point change in the required return moved the value by ₹24 to ₹26 per share, roughly 8%. Intrinsic value is always a range. Anyone who gives you a value to the rupee without showing that range is hiding their assumptions, not displaying precision.

body.title: Show me the math at 10% and 14%

content.caption: Present value of each cash flow (₹ per share; totals use unrounded values)

children.text: Discount factors at 10% are 1.1000, 1.2100, 1.3310, 1.4641 and 1.6105. At 14% they are 1.1400, 1.2996, 1.4815, 1.6890 and 1.9254. Each present value is the cash flow divided by the factor for its year.
Why Price and Value Drift Apart

If intrinsic value only changes when the business outlook changes, why does price move so much more? Because price also absorbs fear, greed, FII selling, index rebalancing, margin calls and the simple need of someone, somewhere, to raise cash today.
Example 1: The Covid-19 crash, March 2020

The Nifty 50 fell from a closing high of about 12,360 in mid-January 2020 to 7,610 on 23 March 2020. Lockdowns genuinely damaged a year or two of earnings. But for most Nifty companies, a year or two is a small slice of a business expected to generate cash for decades. The index was back above 12,000 by November 2020. Price had overshot value on the way down.

stats.label: Back above 12,000
stats.context: Within eight months of the low

children.text: Example 2: Paytm's IPO, November 2021

One 97 Communications, the company behind Paytm, listed in November 2021 at an issue price of ₹2,150 per share, valuing its equity at well over ₹1 lakh crore. The stock closed its first day about 27% below the issue price and traded below ₹500 within roughly a year. The business had not lost more than three quarters of its worth in twelve months. The issue price had assumed far more future cash flow than investors later believed was likely. This time, price had run ahead of value on the way in.

body.text: Neither example means the market is foolish. Sometimes a falling price is correctly telling you that value has dropped, as when a lender's bad loans surface or a regulator restricts a business line. A price move is a prompt to re-check your valuation, never a substitute for one.

children.text: What a Valuation Is Actually Telling You
Every valuation, whether it is a DCF in your spreadsheet, a broker's target price or a P/E comparison on screener.in, is a conditional sentence. Learn to read it that way.

body.label: The honest form of every valuation
body.value: If X happens and I require Y, the share is worth Z
body.context: X is the cash flow forecast, Y is the required return and Z is the value. Change X or Y and Z changes with it.

body.title: What a valuation can and cannot do

columns.label: What it tells you
points: What the business is worth under clearly stated assumptions
Which assumptions matter most to the answer
What the current price implies about the future
Whether today's price gives you a margin of safety

columns.label: What it does not tell you
points: When the price will move toward value
Where the stock will trade in 12 months
Whether your assumptions are correct
Anything useful if the inputs are guesses dressed up as precision

body.text: A broker's 12-month target price is not an intrinsic value. It usually blends a valuation with a view on the multiple the market will pay a year from now. Treat it as one analyst's conditional sentence: read the assumptions in the research report and decide whether you agree with them.

children.text: This is also why valuation feels uncomfortable. It forces you to write down, in numbers, what you believe about a business, in a form where you can be proven wrong. A stock tip never does that.

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Pull up any NSE or BSE company to see its current price and market cap alongside ten years of profits and cash flows. Get used to reading them together: the first is the market's price, the second is the raw material for value.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: A 30% fall
body.question: A stock you follow falls from ₹800 to ₹560 in three months. Nothing about the company's business, debt or management has changed. What can you conclude?
options: Its intrinsic value has fallen by 30%
The gap between price and your estimate of value has moved in your favour, so it deserves a fresh look
Falling stocks should be avoided until the trend reverses
body.explanation: Price fell 30%, but you can only call it undervalued if you had an estimate of value to begin with. If the business is unchanged, your value estimate is broadly unchanged, so the price-to-value gap has widened in your favour. That is a reason to re-check your numbers, not an automatic buy.

body.title: Discounting a single cash flow
body.prompt: You expect to receive ₹500 per share from Tarangini Cold Chain at the end of year 3, and nothing before that. At a 12% required return, what is that ₹500 worth today? Round to the nearest rupee.
body.explanation: ₹500 ÷ (1.12)³ = ₹500 ÷ 1.4049 = ₹355.89, or about ₹356. Waiting three years and bearing the risk costs you roughly ₹144 of value today.

body.title: Discount rate and value
body.textWithBlank: Keeping the expected cash flows the same, a higher discount rate produces a ___ intrinsic value.
body.explanation: A higher required return shrinks every future cash flow more when it is brought back to today. In the Tarangini example, moving from 12% to 14% cut the value from about ₹312 to about ₹288.

body.title: The "cheapest in three years" tip
body.scenario: Karan, a Bengaluru software engineer, spots a mid-cap chemicals stock on screener.in trading at ₹1,450, down 35% from its 52-week high. A WhatsApp investing group calls it "the cheapest it has been in three years" and a finfluencer has posted a target of ₹2,200. Karan has ₹2 lakh sitting in his Zerodha account.
body.prompt: Using only the ideas in this lesson, what should Karan establish before he buys?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Cheap compared to its own past price is not the same as cheap compared to value. A 35% fall says nothing by itself. Karan needs a view on what the business is worth.
2. Find out why the price fell. If a key export market or large customer has dried up, value may have fallen as much as price. If the stock simply fell with the broader mid-cap index, the gap between price and value may genuinely have widened.
3. Read the ₹2,200 target as a conditional sentence with hidden assumptions. What earnings, growth and required return does it rely on? If the finfluencer cannot say, the number carries no information.
4. Estimate a range, not a point. Even a rough range built from expected cash flows and a sensible required return tells him more than any target price.
5. Decide in advance how big a gap is enough. Only if the price sits clearly below the low end of his range does he have a margin of safety. The rest of this course gives him the tools to build that range properly.

points: Price is a fact set by buyers and sellers on NSE and BSE. Intrinsic value is an estimate of what the business is worth to its owners.
Intrinsic value is the present value of the cash a business will generate for its owners, discounted at a rate that reflects time and risk.
Market capitalisation is price multiplied by shares outstanding. A fall in market cap is not the same as a fall in value.
Small changes in assumptions, such as the required return, move value meaningfully, so always think in ranges.
Price and value drift apart through fear, as in March 2020, and through over-optimism, as with Paytm's 2021 IPO price.
Every valuation is a conditional sentence: if these cash flows and this required return, then this value. It never tells you when price will catch up.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Tarangini Cold Chain Ltd and the individuals named are fictional, and their figures are illustrative. Index and IPO figures are approximate and rounded. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
